title: Student Loans (Overseas Debtors Repayment Levy) Bill 2015
short_title: Student Loans (Overseas Debtors Repayment Levy) Bill 2015

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would create a levy for certain student loan borrowers who live overseas.
The Australian Taxation Office would collect the levy using its existing tax administration systems.
The government expects the measure to reduce spending by over $25 million between 2015–16 and 2018–19 and by more than $150 million over ten years.
changes: The bill imposes a repayment levy on overseas residents with HELP or TSL debts.
The levy would apply to both new and existing debts.
Repayment obligations would start only when the borrower earns above the minimum repayment threshold.
summary.affected: Overseas residents with Higher Education Loan Programme (HELP) or Trade Support Loan (TSL) debts.

The majority voted against an [amendment](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2015-11-09.209.1) introduced by Greens Senator [Robert Simms](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/sa/robert_simms). ### What was the amendment? The amendment was about how the bills would apply to people with student debts who already live overseas. It would have meant that the changes made by the bills wouldn't apply to those people so long as they continued to live and work overseas and didn't add to their debts at all (yearly indexation doesn't count as adding to your debt). ### What are the changes made by the bills? **These bills relate to the policy [for requiring Australians working overseas to repay their student debts](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/policies/82).** If made into law, the bills will require Australians living overseas and earning over the threshold (which was $54,126 in 2015–16) to repay their [Higher Education Loan Programme](https://www.education.gov.au/higher-education-loan-program-help) (HELP) debt or [Trade Support Loan](http://www.australianapprenticeships.gov.au/trade-support-loans) (TSL) debt under the same compulsory repayment scheme that applies in Australia. The bills will also require Australians with HELP or TSL debts to notify the Commissioner of Taxation if they plan to be overseas for at least 183 days or if they have been overseas for at least 183 days over any 12 month period. The notification will have to occur either: * no later than seven days after leaving Australia; or * no later than seven days after the end of those 183 days See [StudyAssist](http://studyassist.gov.au/sites/studyassist/helpfulresources/pages/2015%20budget%20-%20student%20overview) for information about when these changes will come into effect. Previously, Australians with HELP or TSL debts who moved overseas didn't have to make any repayments, regardless of how much they earned. speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: The bills require Australians with HELP or trade support loan debts living overseas to repay based on their worldwide income if above the minimum repayment threshold, starting 1 July 2017, with projected savings of over $150 million over 10 years. The legislation also enables data sharing with overseas jurisdictions for debt recovery and prohibits tax deductions for overseas repayments.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: The Student Loans (Overseas Debtors Repayment Levy) Bill 2015 requires Australians living overseas with Higher Education Loan Program or trade support loan debts to repay them under the same obligations as domestic debtors, with repayment commencing only after reaching the minimum threshold, and strengthens the legislative basis and the Australian Taxation Office's capacity to collect the debt.

speeches.speaker: Amanda Rishworth
speeches.brief: Labor supported the Education Legislation Amendment (Overseas Debt Recovery) Bill 2015, which from 1 July 2016 requires HELP and HECS debtors living overseas for six months or more to repay debts at Australian rates if worldwide income exceeds the threshold. The bill is expected to affect 46,000 Australians, with 38,000 making repayments totalling $26 million over four years and saving the Commonwealth $150 million.

speeches.speaker: Joanne Ryan
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the bills, which would affect 46,000 Australians overseas and save $150 million over ten years, but expressed reservations about the government's plans for $100,000 degrees and the need for effective communication to avoid a 30% default rate.

speeches.speaker: Luke Howarth
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of the Education Legislation Amendment (Overseas Debt Recovery) Bill 2015, which requires Australians living overseas to repay their HELP and TSL debts based on worldwide income, with repayments starting above $54,126. The speaker also defended the HECS system, noting the government pays 60% of university fees, and rejected Labor’s claims that degrees would cost $100,000.

speeches.speaker: Craig Kelly
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Education Legislation Amendment (Overseas Debt Recovery) Bill 2015 and the Student Loans (Overseas Debtors Repayment Levy) Bill 2015 are fair and necessary, noting that $800 million in revenue has been lost since 1989 because overseas earners did not repay student debts. He criticised the opposition’s claims about "$100,000 degrees" as a deliberate scare campaign and stated that graduates earning above approximately $50,000 overseas should contribute to the cost of their education.

speeches.speaker: Steve Irons
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Education Legislation Amendment (Overseas Debt Recovery) Bill 2015 and Student Loans (Overseas Debtors Repayment Levy) Bill 2015 close a loophole by requiring Australians living overseas to repay student loans, saving an estimated $25 million from 2015–16 to 2018–19 and over $150 million over 10 years; from 1 January 2016, debtors living overseas for six months or more must notify the ATO, and from 1 July 2017 repayments will be based on income exceeding approximately $54,000.

speeches.speaker: Luke Hartsuyker
speeches.brief: The bills require Australians living overseas for six months or more to repay their Higher Education Loan Program and Trade Support Loans debts based on their income, with data-sharing arrangements with New Zealand and the United Kingdom, and are projected to save over $150 million over ten years.
